Two tests in `tests/integration/tests/task_queue.rs` drive the real loop: 30 tasks run once each and a clean stop gives back no lease; with 6 hanging tasks it holds exactly 4 leases, and on shutdown aborts them after the drain and gives back 4 leases and their attempts. `askhava-server` no longer names `sqlx`. Reason: D-491's point, that a task registers its handler in a shared server file, still holds (`register_handlers()` in `app/server/src/lib.rs`); only the loop body moved, so the tests run the code the worker runs.
- **D-729** Question (T015, October 30, 2026): how does `ops` keep an append-only audit log that holds IDs only (JOB-005, OPS-010, OPS-011, PRIV-028), and who copies it off the database? Choice: `migrations/0021_ops_audit.sql` creates the `ops` schema with the default grants and revokes `UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE` from `askhava_app` on `ops.audit_log` and `ops.switch_history` right after each `CREATE TABLE` (postgres brain P5). Actor and subject are `uuid` columns (row IDs are UUIDs, postgres brain P11); every text column of an audit row is a lower-case code name (`^[a-z][a-z0-9_.]{0,63}$`) checked in Rust (`is_code_name`, names typed `&'static str` so a runtime value is not passed by accident) and by a table `CHECK`, so a phone, email or street address cannot be stored, and a portal field edit logs the field name only (PRIV-028). `ops::api::audit` takes the caller's `PgConnection`, so the audit row commits with the status change (JOB-005, rust brain R11). The export is `export_audit(after, limit)`: rows in `id` order after a cursor, at most 1,000 a page, with `AuditRow::to_json` as the line format (OPS-010). The `id` cursor serves the paged export only: identity values are taken at insert and can commit out of order, so a reader past ID n can miss a row with a lower ID that commits later. The off-database copy (OPS-011, TD-OPS-03's storage stand-in case) is T017's, which owns the storage path and must not read this cursor: it uses a per-row `core.task` or outbox row inserted in the audit row's own transaction (rust brain R11), or reads only below a safe horizon (no transaction older than it still open). T015 enqueues no `core.task` for it, since no handler exists yet and an unhandled kind would dead-letter every row. `ops.alert` holds kind, severity (`critical`, `high`, `normal`) and the subject by ID only; its `id` is a UUID. Pause switches (OPS-003): `ops.pause_switch` (UUID `id`) keyed by name and, for a town or trade, its record ID (`UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT`); `set_switch` changes a switch only when it differs and, in one transaction (`begin`, a savepoint inside the caller's), writes actor and new state to `ops.switch_history` and an `ops.audit_log` row with action `switch_on` or `switch_off`, subject `ops.pause_switch` and the switch row's UUID, and the actor, since every owner action is audit-logged (SEC-006); the action names fit the code-name `CHECK`. A switch never set is off, so turning it off writes nothing, and a repeat of the current state writes nothing. T015 provides only the OPS-003 store; nothing reads a switch yet. Queries sit in `src/service.rs` rather than `src/models.rs` (section 2's layout), because each function is one statement with no orchestration around it. Reason: the requirements as written and the postgres brain P5; the stream split follows the task graph (T017 owns OPS-011's copy). Size: the prompt's budget is 7 files and 450 changed lines; T015 changed its 7 owned files plus shared paths (`Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, the `ops` `CLAUDE.md` and `sqlx.toml`, the integration `Cargo.toml`, `.sqlx/`, `docs/architecture.md`, this file), so the file overrun is in shared files only, and it is about 1,160 changed lines, of which about 308 are generated `.sqlx/` query files and most of the rest the integration tests and the `ops` models; kept as one change because the tables, their API and the append-only tests only work together.
- **D-724** Question (T176, October 30, 2026): how is every server-side fetch of a URL a person or vendor supplied guarded (SEC-041, D-480)? Choice: one function, `askhava_adapters::api::fetch_untrusted(&FetchPolicy, url)`. A `FetchPolicy` lists the allowed hosts (a listed host also allows its subdomains, matched on a dot boundary), a size cap and a timeout; only `https` is fetched. Each hop: the host must be listed and carry no userinfo, `tokio::net::lookup_host` resolves it, every resolved address must pass `is_public_address` (refuses private, loopback, link-local including 169.254.169.254, shared 100.64/10, benchmark, documentation, multicast, reserved, unspecified, IPv6 unique-local and link-local, and the IPv4 inside an IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible or NAT64 address), and the connection goes only to those checked addresses (`resolve_to_addrs`, so no second lookup can rebind). Redirects are not followed by the client; the guard follows at most 3 (`MAX_REDIRECTS`), re-checking each hop the same way, so a redirect off the allowed hosts or to a private address is refused. The body is refused on a `Content-Length` over the cap and otherwise read chunk by chunk and cut at the cap. `FetchPolicy::twilio_media()` allows only `api.twilio.com` and `twiliocdn.com` (Twilio's media redirect target), 10 MB, 20 seconds; review-link callers build their own policy with their review hosts. Tests may add loopback and `http` through the `#[cfg(test)]`-only `with_loopback_for_tests`; private, link-local and metadata addresses stay refused under it. Errors (`FetchError`) carry no URL (PRIV-016). Tests: `app/adapters/src/tests/ssrf_guard.rs` (TD-SEC-20). Reason: checking the name alone, or resolving twice, lets DNS rebinding or a redirect reach the metadata address. Source: `docs/spec/security.md:45`; D-480.
- **D-725** Question (T176, October 30, 2026): what shape do the payments, AI, email, letters, license-source and storage clients take, and where is the email suppression removal (SEC-018, SEC-032, AI-009, BIZ-056, D-492)? Choice: one trait and one client each, re-exported from `api`: `PaymentsAdapter`/`StripePayments` (form posts to `/v1/customers`, `/v1/payment_intents` with `confirm=true`, `/v1/refunds`; `fetch_payment_intent`; IDs and amounts only, metadata `business_id` and `pick_id`), `AiAdapter`/`StandInAi`, `EmailAdapter`/`ResendEmail` (`send_email` to `/emails`; `remove_suppression` as `DELETE /suppressions/{address}`, the address percent-encoded as one segment; T133's fake Resend serves this path and the Phase 2 contract run checks it against Resend's API), `LettersAdapter`/`LobLetters` (`/v1/letters`), `LicenseSource`/`LicenseLists` (read-only `fetch_daily_list` and `lookup_license`; a `file://` base reads fixture lists, `http(s)` the public lists; the live-lookup throttle is `licensing`'s) and `StorageAdapter`/`LocalStorage`. They share `base::VendorHttp`: the base URL is parsed once, path segments are pushed percent-encoded (so a caller's ID cannot change the path), no redirects, 15-second timeout, every outside-acting method takes `&IdempotencyKey` and sends it as `Idempotency-Key`, errors keep only the status. AI-009: `StandInAi::new` accepts only an `http` loopback base URL and sends the fixed non-key `stand-in` as `x-api-key`, so no real AI key or real endpoint is usable during the build; the real client comes with the Phase 2 task that switches on AI-008. The base URL and key settings for these vendors are not parsed here: each consuming task adds its `ASKHAVA_*` keys to core's `KEYS` and checks the URL with `check_base_url`, as `TwilioConfig` does, because `config.rs` is not this task's file. `tokio` moves from a dev-dependency to a dependency of `adapters` (resolution and `spawn_blocking`; already approved). Tests: `ssrf_guard.rs::payments_client_talks_to_the_stand_in` and `email_and_ai_clients_talk_to_the_stand_in` against `python3 -m stand_ins.server`. Source: `docs/spec/security.md:22`; `docs/spec/ai.md:13`; `docs/spec/businesses.md:60`; `docs/architecture.md` section 7; D-453; D-492; D-596.
- **D-726** Question (T176, October 30, 2026): what does the storage adapter do in Phase 1 (PRIV-023, PRIV-029, D-492)? Choice: `LocalStorage` under a `file://` directory: an object name is `/`-separated parts of ASCII letters, digits, `_`, `-` and `.` not starting with a dot (no climbing out), objects are write-once (a second put of the same name is a no-op, so a retry under the same key cannot change what was stored), the write goes to a temporary file named by the idempotency key and is renamed into place, and file work runs in `spawn_blocking` (R10). The Backblaze B2 client with a write-only, prefix-scoped key is added in Phase 2 behind the same trait. Tests: `ssrf_guard.rs::storage_writes_once_and_refuses_unsafe_names`. Source: `docs/architecture.md` section 7 (`storage` row); D-492.
- **D-727** Question (T176 review fixes, October 30, 2026): what closes the security review's gaps in the SEC-041 guard and the vendor clients (D-724, D-725)? Choice: the per-hop client of `fetch_untrusted` and `VendorHttp`'s client are built with `no_proxy()`, so an `HTTP(S)_PROXY` or `ALL_PROXY` in the environment cannot route around the pinned, checked addresses or carry a vendor credential elsewhere (test `ssrf_guard.rs::fetch_and_vendor_clients_ignore_proxy_settings` re-runs the test binary with proxy variables set, since tests never `set_var` (R16); it fails with `no_proxy()` removed); the DNS lookup runs under the policy's timeout (`FetchError::TimedOut`); a URL with any user name or password, or an `https` port other than 443, is refused as `HostNotAllowed` (only the `#[cfg(test)]` loopback allowance permits `http` and other ports); `is_public_address` also refuses IPv4 192.0.0.0/24 and IPv6 6to4 2002::/16, Teredo 2001::/32, site-local fec0::/10, discard 100::/64 and local-use NAT64 64:ff9b:1::/48. `tokio` is a normal dependency of `adapters`, not only a dev-dependency (resolution, `tokio::time::timeout`, `spawn_blocking`; already on the allow-list, no new crate). Open item: the review's finding 12, on how MMS media is fetched through `fetch_untrusted`, is left to the task that wires MMS media download, which must apply it there. Second review follow-up: `FetchPolicy::new` drops an allowed-host entry that is empty, starts or ends with a dot, or has no dot (an empty entry used to match every host ending in a dot, so the policy failed open; a dotless name such as `localhost` or an IPv6 literal cannot be listed); `fetch_untrusted` runs its whole redirect loop under one `tokio::time::timeout(policy.timeout)`, so a chain of slow hops, each under the per-hop limit, is still `TimedOut` (the lookup and per-hop client timeouts stay); IPv6 now passes only inside global unicast 2000::/3, minus 6to4 2002::/16, Teredo 2001::/32 and documentation 2001:db8::/32 (allow-list instead of a block-list, so unique-local, site-local, discard and later-assigned ranges are refused by default). Tests: `ssrf_guard.rs::bad_allowed_host_entries_fail_closed`, `slow_redirect_chains_time_out_overall`, `ipv6_outside_global_unicast_is_refused`; `media_from_a_non_twilio_host_is_refused` lists `127.0.0.1` instead of the now-dropped `localhost` for its loopback case, with the same assertion. Source: `docs/spec/security.md:45`; D-480; D-724.
- **D-728** Question (T176 review fixes, October 30, 2026): what do the payments, letters, AI and storage clients need so their callers' checks hold (PICK-022, SEC-030, SEC-039, SEC-032, AI-009, D-726)? Choice: `PaymentIntent` carries the required `currency`, `customer` and `metadata.pick_id` (`IntentMetadata`), so the release check can compare livemode, customer, amount, currency and pick after the re-fetch, and a body missing one fails with `Decode`; `livemode` is `Option<bool>` with no default, never a silent `false`, and the release check must treat `None` as a mismatch; it is not a required field because the stand-in Stripe (`stand_ins/stripe.py`, a protected path) omits it, which a harness task should fix, after which it can become required. Vendor IDs are checked by `base::is_vendor_id` (prefix, a non-empty tail of letters, digits and `_`, at most 255 characters): `pi_` for `fetch_payment_intent` and `create_refund`, `cus_` and `pm_` for the charge, `ltr_` for `fetch_letter`, else `InvalidId`. `StandInAi::new` accepts only a loopback IP literal, never the name `localhost`. `LocalStorage` writes the temporary file and hard-links it into place (`hard_link` fails when the object exists, so a racing writer can never replace it), then removes the temporary file (replaces D-726's rename). Second review follow-up: the temporary file is `<name>.<key>.part` (appended, so `a.bin` and `a.txt` no longer share one temporary name); a put of a name that exists with the same bytes is a retry and returns `Ok`, one with other bytes returns the new `AdapterError::ObjectExists` instead of a silent `Ok` (this changes `storage_writes_once_and_refuses_unsafe_names`, which had asserted the silent `Ok`; the stored bytes are still checked unchanged). `remove_suppression` refuses, as `InvalidId` and before any request, an address that is not one `@` with text on both sides, so `""`, `.` or `..` can never become a path segment that addresses the whole suppression collection (test `remove_suppression_refuses_non_address_segments`). New tests: suppression removal against a one-request recording server (the stand-in has no suppression route until T133), Lob letters with idempotent replay against the stand-in, license lists from files and over HTTP, refund replay under the same key, malformed IDs. Source: `docs/brains/payments-stripe.md` section 15; `docs/spec/security.md:22`; `docs/spec/ai.md:13`; D-725; D-726.
- **D-734** Question (T017, October 30, 2026): how do the audit stream, the web request log and the AI structured readings reach object storage as they happen when `ops` may call nothing (OPS-010, OPS-011, PRIV-029, D-491, D-729)? Choice: `ops::api::stream_event(db, &StreamEvent)` inserts one `ops.offdb_stream` `core.task` on the caller's connection, so it commits with the row it copies (rust brain R11); `StreamEvent` is `Audit(id)`, `Request { request_id, route, status, at }` or `AiReading { reading_id, fields }`, and AI fields must each be a code name and value, so no AI-written text can enter the stream. T015's audit write now streams: `ops::api::audit` is a wrapper that calls `service::audit` and then `stream_event` (dedupe key `offdb.audit.<id>`), and `ops::api::set_switch` wraps `service::set_switch` in a savepoint and streams the switch's newest audit row, found by joining `ops.pause_switch` (the flip's row lock means no later change of that switch exists); `currval` on the identity sequence was tried and refused, since the app role has no `USAGE` on it. `service.rs` itself is unchanged (not this task's file), so `service::audit` must not be called directly; the note saying so sits on the `use crate::service` line of `ops`' `api.rs` (the module is private, so only `ops` itself could). A request line is never deduplicated, because a client may send its own `x-request-id`, which is recorded only when it parses as a UUID. The writer is `app/server/src/offdb_stream.rs`, registered by `register_handlers(stream)`; it writes `audit/<id 19 digits>.json`, `request/<UTC date>/<task id>.json` and `ai_reading/<id>.json` through `StorageAdapter::put_object` with `IdempotencyKey::derive(ID_SECRET, "offdb.put", [name])`, so a retry is a same-bytes no-op. The `log_request` middleware in `build_router(pool)` (innermost, so it sees `MatchedPath` and the request ID) hands each request's line to `RequestLog`, a bounded channel (1,024 lines) drained by one background task that queues each line with a 2-second limit, so no response waits on a pool connection or an insert; a full channel or a line not queued in time is dropped and counted (`RequestLog::dropped`, a warning at the 1st, 2nd, 4th... drop), and lines still in the channel when the process stops are lost (D-737). `ops` now depends on `core` (layer 0, always allowed). New settings `ASKHAVA_STORAGE_BASE_URL` (checked by `check_base_url`; a `file://` directory in Phase 1) and `ASKHAVA_ID_SECRET`, parsed by `OffDbStream::from_settings` (both trimmed); the worker refuses to start without them, so `docs/deploy.md` (when written) must list both. Due times use the wall clock, since a stream copy is not a business timer. Tests: `tests/integration/tests/offdb_stream.rs`. Source: `docs/spec/ops-recovery.md:15`; `docs/spec/privacy.md:33`; D-729.
- **D-735** Question (T017, October 30, 2026): what is the audit stream's hash chain, how is it checked nightly, and how is the request log kept 30 days (PRIV-029, TD-OPS-19)? Choice: object `audit/<n>.json` holds `line` (the row's `AuditRow::to_json`), `prev_id` (the row before it, 0 at the start) and `prev_sha256` (hex sha256 of that row's serialised line; 64 zeros at the start). The writer cannot read storage (Phase 2's key is write-only), so it takes the previous row from the database (`ops::api::previous_audit_id`, one `max(id) < n` lookup, however far below it is); when row `n-1` is absent and row `n` is younger than 2 minutes the handler fails and retries, because identity IDs can commit out of order (D-729), and after that it links past the gap. A lower ID that commits later than that is reported by the nightly check as a break (a false alarm, never a silent gap); app transactions are bounded by the role's 15-second statement and 30-second idle timeouts (D-699). `verify_audit_chain` walks the audit rows older than an hour in ID order and requires each object to equal the chain object built from the database, so an edited, removed or inserted object fails; it returns the first broken row ID. The nightly `ops.offdb_verify` task (03:00 Arizona, dedupe key `offdb.verify.<date>`; the worker at start and each run before its work queue today's and tomorrow's, D-737) raises a High `ops.audit_chain_broken` alert on a break, as its last step, and, when storage is the local stand-in, removes `request/<date>` folders older than 30 days (`purge_request_log`); with Backblaze B2 the purge is the bucket's lifecycle rule on `request/` and the check reads with a separate read key, both wired in Phase 2 with the 403, versioning and object-lock drill (T134, T109). Known limit: the check walks the whole chain from the first row every night, so its cost grows with the log; a verified watermark (resume from the last row checked and its line hash, stored where the app cannot rewrite it) is a follow-up for when that run gets slow, not built here. Size: the prompt's budget is 3 files and 300 changed lines; this change is about 750 lines in the 3 owned files (the writer, the tests, the `ops` API) plus wiring in shared paths (`lib.rs`, `main.rs`, `worker.rs`, settings keys, Cargo files, one `.sqlx` file, docs), because the three streams, the chain, its check and the purge are one requirement set and only work together; logged rather than split. Source: `docs/spec/privacy.md:33`; `docs/test-design.md` TD-OPS-19; D-492.
- **D-736** Question (T017, October 30, 2026): how does `tests/integration/tests/offdb_stream.rs` test `app/server/src/offdb_stream.rs` when the layer table lets a test-layer crate depend on modules but not on `askhava-server` (`tests/integration/tests/architecture.rs` `allowed`, TD-SEC-10)? Choice: the test compiles the writer file into itself with `#[path = r"../../../app/server/src/offdb_stream.rs"] mod offdb_stream;` (the file names only module and external crates, so it builds in either crate), and the request case builds its router from the same middleware and request-ID layers `build_router` uses; the integration crate gains dev-dependencies `askhava-adapters`, `sha2`, `tower`, `tower-http` and `tracing`, all already approved. The attribute uses a raw string because `scripts/check_rust_rules.py`'s Askama rule (`path = "<file>.<non-HTML extension>"`, meant for `#[template(path = ...)]`) also matches a module path; that is a false positive here, and a harness task should narrow that pattern to `template(` attributes and let test-layer crates depend on `askhava-server` (both protected or locked files this task may not change). Source: `kit/layers.json`; D-479; D-488.
- **D-737** Question (T017 review, October 30, 2026): how do the nightly chain check and the request log survive failure without stopping the schedule, double-alerting or holding up responses (PRIV-029, OPS-011)? Findings: a nightly run that dead-lettered never queued the next (its dedupe key is unique forever); a retried run raised the High alert again; `log_request` waited for a pool connection and an insert (up to the pool's 5-second acquire limit) before the response went. Choice: `schedule_verify(db, now)` queues the runs for `now`'s Arizona date and the next date (one per date, so repeat calls are no-ops), and `ops.offdb_verify` calls it first, before the check, so tomorrow's run exists whatever happens to today's; the run then checks the chain, purges the stand-in's request days, and raises the alert last, so a retry after a failed earlier step raises it once. `log_request` hands its line to `RequestLog` (a bounded channel of 1,024 and one background writer, each line limited to 2 seconds) and never waits; overflow or a timeout drops and counts the line, a loss the request log accepts (it is a 30-day replay aid, not the audit stream, which still commits in the writing transaction). Also: `ASKHAVA_ID_SECRET` is trimmed like the base URL; the predecessor lookup is one `max(id)` query; the tests remove their temporary directories. Tests: `tests/integration/tests/offdb_stream.rs` (the request case waits on the writer; the chain case checks the next run is queued). Source: `docs/spec/privacy.md:33`; `docs/spec/ops-recovery.md:15`; D-734; D-735.
- **D-739** Question (T020, October 30, 2026): how is the test-control router kept out of the release build and locked in test builds (SEC-035, SEC-002, D-480, D-491)? Choice: `app/core/src/test_control.rs` re-exports `TestControl`, `TestControlError` and `TEST_CONTROL_COMPILED` through `core::api`. Without core's `test-control` feature, `TestControl::from_settings` reads nothing, never fails, and returns a router with no routes and the system clock, so every `/__test/*` path is 404 under every `APP_ENV`; the routes, the bearer check and the stand-in client are inside a `#[cfg(feature = "test-control")]` module, so the release binary carries none of them. `server` merges `TestControl::router()` in `build_router(pool, test_control)` unconditionally (server may not define a feature, T175's architecture test), and the `worker` takes `TestControl::clock()`. With the feature on, the router refuses `APP_ENV` `test` and `live` (`WrongEnvironment`) and needs `ASKHAVA_TEST_CONTROL_SECRET` of at least 32 characters (both keys are added to `settings::KEYS`); every request under `/__test/` passes a `layer` (not a `route_layer`, D-742) that compares `Authorization: Bearer <secret>` without early exit and answers a wrong or missing secret with 404, the same as an absent route, so a probe learns nothing. Routes: `GET /__test/clock`, `POST /__test/clock/advance` (`{"seconds": n}`, `deny_unknown_fields`, at most 366 days, forward only) and `GET /__test/messages?to=&key=`, which calls the Twilio stand-in's `GET .../Messages.json?To=&MessageKey=` (base `ASKHAVA_TWILIO_BASE_URL`, default `http://127.0.0.1:4010/twilio`, checked by `check_base_url`) and returns only its `messages`, never the `messaging` tables. The HTTP client is `reqwest` as an optional dependency of `core` turned on only by the feature (`test-control = ["dep:reqwest"]`; reqwest is already approved and in `Cargo.lock`, so no new library; core is the one crate the architecture test lets hold an optional dependency). The feature is enabled only on the command line (`--features askhava-core/test-control`), never by a dependency line, so `cargo build` of the binaries cannot pick it up by feature unification; `tests/security/tests/control_router_absent.rs` fails if any manifest other than core's `[features]` line names it. Its feature-on cases return early in the default build and run under `cargo test -p askhava-security --test control_router_absent --features askhava-core/test-control`; `Ci` and `smoke.sh` (protected) run only the default build, so the feature-on cases first run in `Ci` when T173's e2e job builds with the feature: a harness follow-up should add that one command to `Ci`. Reason: SEC-035 asks for compile-time absence, not a runtime switch (the D-480 finding); one always-present entry point keeps `server` free of features. Source: `docs/spec/security.md:39`; `docs/test-design.md:75`; D-480; D-491.
- **D-740** Question (T020, October 30, 2026): what does "advance the clock" move, given that timers run in the separate `worker` process (SEC-035, JOB-006, JOB-007)? Choice: in a `test-control` build the clock is the system clock plus a forward-only offset in whole seconds, not a stopped `ManualClock`, so leases, polls and timeouts keep running in real time during an e2e run. When `ASKHAVA_TEST_CONTROL_CLOCK_FILE` is set, the offset lives in that file (written to `<file>.next` then renamed into place) and each `now()` reads it, so the web process that serves the router and the worker that claims due tasks see the same time; without it the offset is in memory and moves only the web process. The few-byte read on each `now()` happens only in test-control builds; the release clock is `SystemClock`. T227's `webserver.ts` gives both binaries the same secret and the same clock file. Reason: a clock advance that the worker cannot see would never fire a timer. Source: `docs/spec/security.md:39`; `docs/brains/rust-production.md` section 3; D-491.
- **D-741** Question (T020, October 30, 2026): what TypeScript tooling sits at the repository root, and how does a spec reach the test-control router (D-453, SEC-035)? Choice: `package.json` (private, `"type": "module"`, Node 22 or later) pins exactly the section 11 versions, `typescript` 6.0.3, `@playwright/test` 1.64.1, `@axe-core/playwright` 4.13.0, `eslint` 10.12.0 and `typescript-eslint` 8.71.2, with `package-lock.json` committed (`npm audit --audit-level=low`: 0 vulnerabilities on October 30, 2026), and the scripts `typecheck` (`tsc --noEmit`) and `lint` (`eslint .`); no `@types/node`, so no file here reads `process.env`. `tsconfig.json` is strict (plus `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`), `noEmit`, over `tests/e2e`, `tests/a11y` and `app/*/static`; T173 adds the `build` script that emits the static `.js`. `eslint.config.js` applies typescript-eslint's `strictTypeChecked` and `stylisticTypeChecked` to every `.ts` file. `tests/e2e/fixtures.ts` exports `test` (Playwright's, extended with the `control` fixture: `now()`, `advanceClock(seconds)`, `sentTexts({to, key})`) and `expect`; the per-run secret is the worker-scoped option `controlSecret`, which T227's `playwright.config.ts` sets to the value it gave the web binary, and requests go to the config's `baseURL`; a missing or short secret fails the fixture with a message saying where to set it. Reason: specs import one place, and the secret flows from the config that starts the binaries. Source: `docs/architecture.md` section 11; `docs/test-design.md:75`; D-453.
- **D-742** Question (T020 review fixes, October 30, 2026): what closes the review's gaps in the test-control router (D-739, D-740, D-727)? Choice: the bearer check is a `layer`, not a `route_layer`, and a `/__test/{*rest}` catch-all answers 404, so every request under `/__test/` (a wrong method or an unknown path included) meets the check and an unauthenticated one gets 404 (on axum 0.8.9 the `route_layer` version already answered a wrong method 404; the test now guards it either way). `control_router_absent.rs` sends every request through the test-control router merged into an empty `Router`, as `askhava_server::build_router` merges it; it cannot call `build_router` itself, because T175's layer table lets a test-layer crate depend on modules only, never on `server` (the first attempt's `askhava-server` dev-dependency failed `td_sec_10_workspace_obeys_the_layer_table`, D-743). The sent-log client has a 10-second timeout and `no_proxy()` (D-727), and a client that fails to build is `TestControlError::HttpClient`. The clock keeps the largest offset it has seen, so a garbled or unreadable clock file never moves time back; an advance takes an exclusive lock on `<file>.lock` (std `File::lock`), so two processes' advances both count, and refuses (500) to overwrite a garbled file. The test-control secret, clock file and Twilio base are parsed from the raw pairs inside `mod enabled`, not as typed `Settings` fields, because a release build must carry no code that reads them; `Settings::from_pairs` only accepts the keys (`settings::KEYS`), and the release build's `TestControl::from_settings` ignores them. Reason: SEC-035 asks that a probe learn nothing and that the router be absent in the shipped app, which only a test through the real router shows. Source: `docs/spec/security.md:39`; D-727; D-739; D-740.
- **D-743** Question (T020 retry, October 30, 2026): the first attempt failed `Ci` (Checks and Coverage) at `td_sec_10_workspace_obeys_the_layer_table`, because `tests/security` named `askhava-server` as a dev-dependency and `kit/layers.json` allows a test-layer crate only module crates; how does TD-SEC-15 still test the router as the app serves it? Choice: `askhava-security`'s dev-dependencies are `askhava-core`, `axum`, `tokio` and `tower` (all already in `[workspace.dependencies]`; no new library), and the test merges `TestControl::router()` into an empty `Router`, which is exactly what `build_router(pool, test_control)` does before its layers (the layers add no route and no fallback). `askhava-server` stays out of `[workspace.dependencies]`. The protected layer table is not changed. Since T017 `build_router` takes the app pool first, so `server` passes `build_router(pool, control.router())` and the `worker` takes `TestControl::clock()` for both the claim loop and the off-database stream. Reason: the layer rule is locked; the merge is the only part of `build_router` the test-control routes depend on. Source: `kit/layers.json`; `tests/integration/tests/architecture.rs`; D-739; D-742.
- **D-744** Question (T021, October 30, 2026): how is `categories.yaml` loaded so a category's switch stays an owner setting and a category not confirmed stays off (LIC-002, LIC-003, LIC-004, LIC-005, AI-017)? Choice: `catalog::api::load_embedded` parses the file compiled into the build (`include_str!`, so no folder is needed at run time) and upserts `catalog.category`, `job_type`, `license_rule`, `fee_rule` and `not_offered`. A new category starts with the file's `enabled`; an existing category keeps its stored switch on reload, so a reload never undoes the owner's logged change. `parse` forces off any category whose code or name matches the not-offered list and refuses a duplicate code, an unknown license kind, quote format or job-type kind, a fee tier outside $25 to $75, or a per-job-type entry naming a job type the category lacks. A category absent from the file is never stored and reads as off. Reason: the file is the reviewed K2b list; the switch is a setting. Source: `docs/spec/licensing.md:5`-`docs/spec/licensing.md:9`; `docs/spec/ai.md:21`; D-202.
- **D-745** Question (T021, October 30, 2026): who may switch a category and what keeps it off until confirmed (LIC-002, LIC-003, LIC-004, AI-017)? Choice: `set_category_enabled` accepts only `Actor::Owner` (`OwnerOnly`), refuses a not-offered kind (`NotOffered`) and a ROC or ROC-and-agency category with no resolved class (`LicenseUnresolved`, which keeps garage doors off until a class is confirmed in the file), and writes the column change and an `ops` audit row (`catalog.category_switched`, status `on`/`off`) in one transaction; a repeat writes nothing. Only the owner switches a category, including one the file left unconfirmed (`enabled: false`): the owner may switch it on if it is offered and its class is resolved, and no worker, timer or AI can; the one system switch is the reload's switch-off (D-747). No catalog function takes a license class, so the AI cannot set one. Reason: LIC-002 asks for a logged settings change with no code change; AI-017 forbids a guessed class. Source: `docs/spec/licensing.md:6`; `docs/spec/ai.md:21`.
- **D-746** Question (T021, October 30, 2026): which of the architecture's catalog tables does T021 build (`docs/architecture.md` section 3 lists `catalog.setting` and `catalog.setting_history`)? Choice: T021 builds `category`, `job_type`, `license_rule`, `fee_rule` and `not_offered` (migration `0027_catalog_module.sql`). The category switch's history is the `ops.audit_log` row, so no separate history table is added for it; `setting` and `setting_history` (fee mode and numeric settings) are left to the task that first needs a non-category setting. The intake questions and their card-field flag are T177's. `launch_open` and `handyman` limits are stored only as far as LIC-001 needs (`handyman_allowed`, `construction_type`). Reason: keep the task small and the history in one append-only place. Source: `docs/architecture.md` section 3; D-202.
- **D-747** Question (T021, October 30, 2026): what does a reload do to a stored switch (LIC-002, LIC-003, LIC-004, AI-017)? Choice: a reload still never switches a category on, but in the same transaction it switches off, with an `Actor::System` audit row (`catalog.category_switched`, `on` to `off`) each, every stored category that is now on the file's not-offered list, has a ROC kind with no classes, or whose code the file no longer lists, and it deletes `not_offered` names the file no longer lists. `set_enabled` flips the column with `UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND enabled = NOT $2` inside its transaction and writes the audit row only when a row changed, so two concurrent switches log once. `parse` also refuses what the table checks refuse (an agency kind without an agency, an agency on another kind, classes on a non-ROC kind). Reason: a list or class change in the reviewed file must be able to turn a category off without a code change, and a check must not depend on a stale read. Source: `docs/spec/licensing.md:6`-`docs/spec/licensing.md:9`; `docs/spec/ai.md:21`.
- **D-748** Question (T021, October 30, 2026): who calls `catalog::api::load_embedded` at start-up? Choice: no task wires it in T021, because `app/server` opens no application database pool yet (`main.rs` runs only the migration release step). The first task that gives the server or worker an application pool at start-up (the composition task that builds the pool) calls `load_embedded` once after migrations and before serving; until then the catalog tables are empty and every category reads as off, which is the safe state. Reason: wiring it here would add a pool to a shared path out of scope. Source: `docs/spec/ai.md:21`; `app/catalog/CLAUDE.md`.
- **D-754** Question (T177, October 30, 2026): how does `catalog` load the question bank, and where is it kept? Choice: `question_bank.rs` parses the compiled-in `docs/catalog/question_bank.yaml` in memory (`api::question_bank`, `api::parse_question_bank`); nothing is stored in a table, because the bank is reviewed text read word for word and a table would add a second copy to drift. `parse_bank` refuses a size band without one `band_floor` per option, photos without a `kb_trade`, an `ask_if` answer number beyond the option count plus one (the app adds a "Not sure" answer, so the number one past the options is allowed), a set outside 3 to 8 questions, a question missing a language, unequal or one-sided option lists, a card field or size band with no options, a repeated id, a condition on a later question or a non-existent answer number, more than 3 photos, a set for an unknown category and an enabled category with no set. The `kb_trade` file and photo-id checks stay in `scripts/check_catalog.py`. Reason: TD-LIC-24 asks the loader to refuse what the script refuses without reading the trade files at run time. Source: `docs/spec/licensing.md:44`.
- **D-755** Question (T177, October 30, 2026): how is the no-warranty rule (LIC-042) enforced at load? Choice: `loader::covers_warranty` matches "warrant", "protection plan", "service contract", "guarantee", "guaranty" and "garantía" in a category's code, name, job types and keywords, and in each question-set code; `parse` and `parse_bank` return `Invalid`. The not-offered list and free question text are not scanned, so a plain question such as "how old is it" is unaffected. Reason: the rule bans covering a warranty as a category, job type or offer; scanning every sentence would block legitimate wording. Source: `docs/spec/licensing.md:46`; D-376.
- **D-756** Question (T177, October 30, 2026): must all five split categories carry repair, replace and install kinds? Choice: no. T233 set kinds on every job type of the five split categories, but plumbing and heating and cooling have no install job type yet; that is a deferral, not a license-rule ban: adding one needs a `scope_tags` row in `docs/catalog/license_map.yaml` (D-605, a follow-up). Electrical holds all three kinds; roof repair and painting hold repair and replace. `parse` refuses an unknown kind and the test checks each group has repair and replace and that every job type has a kind. Reason: LIC-041 says "where the license rule allows", and the install rows are a later catalog task. Source: `docs/spec/licensing.md:45`; D-493, D-605.
- **D-759** Question (T026, October 30, 2026): what shape does the template registry take, and how are template IDs and placeholders written? Choice: `app/messaging/templates/en.json` and `es.json` are objects keyed by template ID (snake_case); each entry holds `audience` (`homeowner` or `business`), `segments` (the count recorded for TXT-044) and `text`, with `{name}` placeholders (not the spec's `<n>` style, which a scan would read as markup); Spanish entries also hold `draft: true`. `Registry::parse` refuses a kind missing a language, a Spanish entry not marked draft, an English one marked draft, a differing audience and any text not beginning "Ask Hava:"; later tasks add only their own keys, in both files (D-491). Reason: TXT-001, TXT-003 and WORD-008 become load-time checks, so a bad file cannot ship. Source: `docs/spec/messaging.md:5`, `docs/spec/messaging.md:7`, `docs/spec/wording.md:12`.
- **D-760** Question (T026, October 30, 2026): how does the code decide Spanish, and which texts stay on while "Spanish conversations" is off? Choice: `language_for(id, wanted, spanish_on)` gives Spanish only when the person's own language is Spanish and either the setting is on or the Spanish entry carries `spanish_stays_on: true`; the caller supplies the language per person, so an owner phone in English and a team phone in Spanish differ (BIZ-018). The flag is set on `emergency_911`, `help_reply` (the AYUDA reply), `opt_out_confirmation` and `spanish_not_yet` (TXT-041); the INT-037 question gets its flag in the task that adds it. The setting itself (owner portal, with the translation-review gate of TXT-039) is read by the caller and passed in; this task stores nothing. Reason: the stay-on list lives beside each text, so adding a text never needs a Rust edit. Source: `docs/spec/messaging.md:43`; D-427.
- **D-761** Question (T026, October 30, 2026): how are segments counted for TXT-044 when a template has placeholders? Choice: `count_segments` counts the template as written, each `{name}` counting its own characters, with a GSM-7 table including the extension characters at 2 units; the registry records that count as `segments` and the test fails if the counted value is above it. The first values recorded: English consent 2 segments (295 characters) and Spanish consent 2 (303), both GSM-7; the Spanish opt-out, HELP, 911 and other texts with accented letters outside GSM-7 are UCS-2 and reported, never failed. Reason: the real length depends on filled values, so the template count is the part a change can control; the check is a floor on deliberate growth, not a length guarantee. Source: `docs/spec/messaging.md:48`; D-490, D-491.
- **D-762** Question (T026, October 30, 2026): where does the template scan live and what does it ban? Choice: `tests/docs/test_template_scan.py` reads both JSON files and fails on an emoji code point, any link whose host is not askhava.com (scheme optional), a host on a list of public shorteners, an ROC link other than askhava.com/help/roc-complaint, promotion wording (promo, discount, coupon, special offer, limited time, "save this number", referral, "on sale", "a deal", "% off" and Spanish equivalents), warranty wording (TD-LIC-18), "reply CANCEL" (also text or send, and Spanish) and a text not beginning "Ask Hava:"; it plants each violation to prove it is caught. Reason: TD-TXT-02 is a data scan, and Python keeps it independent of the Rust parser that loads the files. Source: `docs/spec/messaging.md:9` to `docs/spec/messaging.md:14`.
- **D-763** Question (T026, October 30, 2026): which text kinds exist in the first registry, and how good are the Spanish drafts? Choice: sixteen kinds: `consent` (CON-031) and the stay-on set of TXT-041 (`opt_out_confirmation`, `help_reply`, `emergency_911`, `spanish_not_yet`), which the tests name because TXT-039 and TXT-044 force them, plus `start_reply`, `under_18`, `request_out` (TXT-032), `first_quote` (TXT-016), `all_quotes_in` (TXT-042), `caller_missed` (TXT-030), `problem_reply` (TXT-029), `close_howto` and `cost_answer` (CON-034, each ending with its fixed "If that doesn't fix it..." sentence), `business_no_call_reminder` (TXT-026, with the calling-hours and 2-attempts sentences) and `business_pick_waiting`. Finished to spec: `consent`, `close_howto`, `cost_answer`, `business_no_call_reminder`, `opt_out_confirmation`. Placeholder wording the owning task finalises: `help_reply` (CON-018's help email, Canadian roaming line and the "or within 24 hours if your job is urgent" half belong to the HELP task, T030, which also adds the away-setting variant), and the other kinds' wording (TXT-016, TXT-029, TXT-030, TXT-032, TXT-042 and the business notices) is checked by their owning tasks; the behaviour tests use planted JSON, not these keys. The CON-034 and TXT-026 added Spanish sentences are AI drafts. Spanish wording is exact where the spec gives it and an AI draft elsewhere, all marked `draft` for native-speaker review and, for the stay-on texts, the two-AI back-translation check before launch (TXT-039); that check is not done here. Reason: a registry with fewer kinds than the spec lists is incomplete, so the rest follow in their own tasks, each adding both languages. Source: `docs/spec/messaging.md:5`, `docs/spec/messaging.md:43`.
- **D-749** Question (T022, October 30, 2026): how is the contact vault stored, keyed and read, given `docs/architecture.md` sections 3 and 8 (PRIV-001 to PRIV-004, PRIV-024)? Choice: `privacy.contact` holds one sealed `bytea` column per field (`name`, `phone`, `email`, `address`, `onsite_contact`); a sealed value is a 2-byte big-endian key version, a random 96-bit nonce (`aes-gcm`'s `Nonce::generate()`, the OS source through `getrandom`) and the AES-GCM ciphertext under a 256-bit `VAULT_KEY`, with associated data `privacy.contact|<column>|<row id>|v<version>`; a generated column `oldest_key_version` (through the immutable `privacy.sealed_version`) finds the rows a rotation still has to move. `VAULT_KEY` and `VAULT_INDEX_KEY` are each a comma-separated list of `<version>:<base64 of 32 bytes>`, the highest version active and every listed version readable; `Vault::new` refuses a malformed or repeated entry, a key shared between the two variables, and a key whose text appears in the database credential. The blind index `privacy.contact_index` keeps one HMAC-SHA256 digest per contact, purpose and index-key version, under a key derived as HMAC(`VAULT_INDEX_KEY` vN, `<purpose>|vN`) (`homeowner-phone`, `sender-dir`, `email`); a lookup tries every version, and `rotate_batch` re-seals each row and rebuilds its digest under the active versions, audited as `privacy`'s rotation read. Plaintext reads go through grants (`models::GRANTS`): `messaging` send (every field) and inbound (name, phone), `calls` bridge (phone) and read-back (name, address), `picks` release (name, email, address, on-site contact, never the phone, PICK-023), the homeowner realm's own record (every field), the owner realm's call-back alert and help request (name, phone, email), and `privacy`'s rotation; `read_contact` serves only `messaging` and `calls`, and the release and realm reads take `ReleaseProof`, `HomeownerSessionProof` or `OwnerSessionProof` (with `OwnerPurpose`). Each read writes one `ops.audit_log` row per field (action `vault_read.<reader>.<purpose>`, subject `privacy.contact`, field name) and its hourly count in one transaction that commits before plaintext is returned. `privacy.read_count` is a table section 3's list does not name; that list is locked, so this entry records it and the next plan change should add it. Reason: per-row, per-column associated data is what makes a copied ciphertext fail (TD-PRIV-01); a version per value lets v1 and v2 coexist during the drill (TD-PRIV-09); grants bound the fields as well as the reader. Source: `docs/spec/privacy.md:6`, `docs/spec/privacy.md:28`, `docs/architecture.md:280`.
- **D-750** Question (T022, October 30, 2026): how does SEC-047's read-rate alarm count, and what is an unknown purpose? Choice: every plaintext read adds 1 to `privacy.read_count` for its grant's action and the UTC hour; `check_read_rates(hour)` compares each count of that hour with the mean hourly count of the same action over the 336 hours before it, floored at 1 read per hour (`BASELINE_FLOOR`), and raises one High `privacy.vault_read_spike` alert (subject the `privacy.read_count` row) for each count above 3 times that, marking the row so a second run of the same hour raises nothing. A read whose reader, purpose or any requested field is not a grant (for example `calls` asking to send, or `read_contact` claiming the release or a portal realm) is refused before anything is read and raises a High `privacy.vault_read_unregistered` alert at once. The hourly run of `check_read_rates` is not yet scheduled: `privacy` exposes it, and the task that registers the hourly `core.task` timers wires it. Reason: without a floor a reader's first reads after launch would each alert; with it, a burst above 3 reads in an hour against an empty fortnight still alerts. Source: `docs/spec/security.md:51`.
- **D-751** Question (T022, October 30, 2026): where are the capability reads tested, when the proofs can only be built inside `privacy`, the mints are once per process, and D-597 bans `ReleaseMint`, `release_mint`, `SessionMint` and `session_mint` from the test crates? Choice: the release, homeowner-realm and owner-realm reads are tested in a `#[cfg(test)] mod realm_tests` at the end of `app/privacy/src/api.rs`, which builds proofs by struct literal (its parent module's private fields), so neither mint is spent; the one test there that calls `session_mint()` (and proves a second call panics) is the only caller in the privacy unit-test binary, and `release_mint()`'s once-test stays T192's (`app/privacy/src/tests/release_mint_once.rs`). T022 owns no `src/tests/` file, so an inline module is the only in-crate place; the vault itself is tested from `tests/integration/tests/vault.rs` and the reader scan from `tests/security/tests/vault_readers.rs`. Reason: SEC-046 and TD-SEC-25 need a homeowner session shown to read only its own record, which no crate outside `privacy` can construct. Source: D-488, D-597, `docs/architecture.md:195`.
- **D-752** Question (T022 review fixes, October 30, 2026): what closes the fresh-eyes review's gaps in the contact vault (D-749, D-750, D-751)? Choice: `read_for_release` takes its `ReleaseProof` by value, so one proof opens one release, and writes one more `ops.audit_log` row (action `vault_read.picks.release`, subject `picks.pick` and the proof's pick ID) beside the per-field rows, tying the read to its pick (SEC-030, PRIV-003); every plaintext read refuses with `VaultError::InTransaction` when the caller's connection is already inside a transaction, since that caller's rollback could undo the audit rows after the plaintext left (PRIV-003); `Vault::new` also finds a key in the database credential when it is percent-encoded (`%2B`, `%2F`, `%3D`, either case), unpadded or in the URL-safe alphabet (PRIV-002); a unique violation on the blind index's primary key, from two contacts racing for one phone, is `PhoneTaken`, not a database error; only `rotate_batch`'s re-seal locks the row (`FOR UPDATE`), plain reads do not; and the unregistered-purpose High alert carries subject kind `vault_read.<reader>.<purpose>` and the contact's ID, so the alert names who asked and why (SEC-047). Each has a test in `tests/integration/tests/vault.rs` or `app/privacy/src/api.rs` `realm_tests`. The review's other, low items are left as they were; nothing here changes the spec, the test design or a locked file.
- **D-753** Question (T022 second review, October 30, 2026): what closes the second fresh-eyes review of the contact vault (D-752)? Choice: (1) a `ReleaseProof` names the contact as well as the pick: `ReleaseMint::mint(pick_id, contact_id, basis)`, `ReleaseProof::contact_id()`, and `read_for_release(db, vault, proof, fields)` drops its contact-ID parameter and opens only the contact the proof names, so a valid proof for one pick can never open another homeowner's contact (SEC-030); no crate outside `privacy` calls either yet, so no caller changes, and T189's minter passes the pick's contact ID. (2) The unregistered-purpose refusal refuses a connection inside a transaction (`VaultError::InTransaction`) before it raises its alert, as the read does, so a caller's rollback cannot undo the alert (SEC-047). (3) The in-transaction check also asks the server: after sqlx's own depth counter, a transaction-local `set_config('askhava.vault_probe', ...)` that is still set at the next statement means a block is open, which catches a raw `BEGIN` sqlx does not count; it raises no error, so nothing reaches the server log (PRIV-003). (4) `rotate_batch` selects contacts by stale `homeowner-phone` digests only, the one purpose `reseal` rebuilds, so a stale digest of another purpose cannot keep a batch from reaching 0 (PRIV-024). (5) `check_read_rates` rounds its time down to the UTC hour in SQL, so a caller passing a time inside the hour checks that hour (SEC-047). (6) The reader scan in `tests/security/tests/vault_readers.rs` drops nested block comments and blanks raw, byte and character literals (a `'"'` no longer opens a string), and counts a `portals` file as business realm when its path or any identifier in it holds both `business` and `session` (PRIV-004, SEC-046). Each has a test in `tests/integration/tests/vault.rs`, `tests/security/tests/vault_readers.rs` or `app/privacy/src/api.rs` `realm_tests`. Nothing here changes the spec, the test design or a locked file. Source: the review of T022, D-752.
- **D-764** Question (T027, October 30, 2026): how does `rules::decide` find the next send time, and what do the DST days do (QH-001, QH-002, QH-006, QH-009)? Choice: the allowed stretch always opens when one zone reaches 08:00 local, so the hold ends at the earliest 08:00 in Arizona or the recipient's zone, within three days, at which both zones are inside 8:00 to before 20:00; zone rules come from `jiff` with the bundled database (already approved, no new crate). Reason: exact for half-hour zones (709) and both daylight-saving change days, and no minute scanning.
- **D-765** Question (T027, October 30, 2026): which table covers the area-code zones (QH-003, D-100, D-139)? Choice: `app/messaging/area_codes.json`, `{zone: [codes]}`, 406 US, territory and Canadian codes. A code that spans zones is listed under each zone and `decide` requires every zone to be open, the stricter reading of QH-001: 928 (Navajo Nation keeps daylight saving: Phoenix and Denver), 850 and 906 (Eastern and Central), 208 (Denver and Los Angeles), 541 and 775 (Los Angeles and Denver), 605, 701, 308, 785, 620 and 432 (Central and Denver), 812, 930, 270, 364 and 931 (Eastern and Central), 807 (Toronto and Winnipeg), 709 (St. Johns and Goose Bay), 250 (Vancouver and Dawson Creek), 907 (Anchorage and Adak), 867 (Edmonton, Iqaluit, Rankin Inlet, Whitehorse). The parser rejects a repeat within one zone, a bad code or an unknown zone. New codes added from knowledge of the public plan: 945, 557, 464, 235, 826, 584, 257, 468; codes not known with confidence (382, 683, 327, 861, 357, 728 and others) are left out and so are refused. Risk: the table is written from memory and split-code lists may be incomplete; a missed zone could text outside a zone's window, and a missing code only refuses a text. Caribbean NANP codes (D-100) are absent. A number that is not `+1` plus ten digits, or whose code is absent, is an error for every kind, including the exceptions. Reason: one rule (D-139); the table is the refusal point. Casey or the owner should confirm the table against the NANPA list before Gate C; it was written from memory of the public plan.
- **D-766** Question (T027, October 30, 2026): how are QH-004's exceptions coded, where the sentence is ambiguous? Choice: `Safety911`, `KeywordReply`, `PickCode` and `AfterHoursNotice` (INT-033, which is sent before any emergency choice, D-271) go at any hour; a `DirectReply` goes only when 0 <= age < 15:00 from the inbound text (D-101); `Quote`, `JobQuestion` and `PickStep` go at night only when the job is an emergency; `JobCard` and `ConfirmRequest` go at night only by email, for an emergency job, to a business that ticked after-hours and a person with "Emergency emails at any hour" on (D-054, D-346). `Quote` is the first-quote text and `QuoteCount` the "You now have N quotes" update (TXT-017); both follow the emergency rule. Everything else, including a non-emergency first-quote text, is held. Alerts to Casey are not texts (D-314) so have no kind. Reason: each follows QH-004 and TD-QH-02 literally.
- **D-767** Question (T027, October 30, 2026): which zone governs a business email (QH-005)? Choice: the area code of the receiving person's or business's `+1` phone, as for a text, together with Arizona; `Outgoing.channel` only matters for the card and confirm night exception. QH-004 and QH-005 read differently on channels: QH-005 says every channel of one notice is held together, yet QH-004 lets a job card or confirm request go at night by email only. Decided: `decide` is called per channel, so an emergency card goes by email at night while its text channel is held to the window start, which QH-004's "by email" requires; with no exception both channels get the same `until`. An email needs a recipient `+1` phone on file to judge the zone; an email-only recipient with no phone is refused as `NotNorthAmerican` (the caller supplies the phone it holds for the business or person). Reason: QH-005 says emails follow the rule "exactly as texts", and a notice's channels share one clock because one `decide` call answers for the notice.
- **D-768** Question (T027, October 30, 2026): how do merging, dropping and retries work without reading `jobs` (TXT-025, QH-007, QH-008, D-158, D-461)? Choice: `plan_release(held, job_closed)` takes the sending module's `job_closed` check as a parameter: a held message for a closed job is `Drop` unless `announces_close`; otherwise held `Kind::Update`s for one (job, recipient) become one `Merged` list (oldest first) whose text the sender renders; `Kind::QuoteCount` updates merge in the same group as `Kind::Update` (TXT-025 merges update texts; the first-quote text `Kind::Quote` does not); closing texts and other kinds are never merged. `retry` is `decide` judged at the retry instant. Reason: `messaging` cannot read `jobs` (architecture section 4); one decision function for first sends and retries keeps QH-008 true by construction.
- **D-794** Question (harness plan change, October 30, 2026; a regression from D-723): why did every backup-runner job since #121 end as a failure in "Start the next cycle at once when this one cleared the way (D-500)", and why did a lane freed by another lane's merge still sit idle? What happened (read from runs 41113112688 and 41113143461 and their logs): the step printed "chain: no" and then bash stopped with "syntax error near unexpected token `('" (exit code 2). D-723 added a comment inside the refill snippet, which is Python in a single-quoted `python3 -c '...'`; the comment's apostrophe in "another lane's merge" ended the single quote, so bash read the rest of the snippet as shell. The refill loop never ran, so after every non-hand-off cycle a freed lane waited for a pull request event or the hourly tick, and every job showed red. The snippet tests in `tests/test_runner_two_lanes.py` cut the Python out of the step and run it alone, so they could not see a shell parse error. Kind: bug; no section 7 line changes, `kit/plan.lock` is written and unchanged (no locked file changes), and `.github/` and `tests/` change only in this logged plan change. Options weighed: (a) only reword the comment: fixes this run but leaves the same slip open for any future edit; (b) move the snippets into a Python file under `runner/`: a larger change to a locked workflow for a one-word bug; (c) reword the comment and add a test that runs `bash -n` over every `run:` step of every workflow. Choice (c): the comment reads "may have resolved the merge of another lane", and the new `tests/test_workflow_shell.py` parses each bash `run:` step in `.github/workflows/*.yml` with `bash -n` after replacing every `${{ ... }}` expression with a plain word, plus a check that the test itself catches an apostrophe inside a single-quoted snippet. The new test fails on the workflow as it was on `main` and passes after the fix. No existing test assertion changes. Reason: the chain step is the refill path for every cycle that does not hand off; a parse check of every step is the cheapest guard against the whole class of quoting slips. Source: `BUILD_BRIEF.md:224`; `BUILD_BRIEF.md:490`; D-500; D-620; D-723.
- **D-795** Question (T217, October 30, 2026): how does the stage 2 sentinel scan (TD-PRIV-02; PRIV-016, PRIV-019) work, and which sentinel street does it plant, given that the task goal names "1 Sentinel Way" (`kit/tasks.json` T217) while the fixture crate's fixed sentinel is "1 Canary Way" (D-647, `tests/fixtures/src/fake_data.rs` `SENTINEL_STREET`)? Choice: the scan plants the fixture's sentinels, street included, so T120's journey scan and this one share one set of values and no second street constant exists; the goal's street wording is read as "the sentinel street". `tests/security/tests/sentinel_db_logs.rs` stores the sentinel through `store_contact` as the app role (phone typed `+1 928 555 0199`), finds it by phone, reads it under the messaging send grant, is refused under an unregistered purpose (alert row) and is refused a second store (`PhoneTaken`, logged once with `tracing::error!`); sends one request with the sentinels in path, query and a header through the `build_router` layers; and runs every queued `core.task` through the off-database stream handlers into a temporary `file://` stand-in (the writer compiled in place, D-736). The JSON log is captured from `json_layer` with no level filter (sqlx statement logs included); the Sentry stub is a `sentry::Transport` that keeps every envelope, behind `sentry_options` and the `ErrorLayer` as `logging::init` wires them. It then searches every `pg_tables` table but `privacy.contact` (each row as `row_to_json`, so bytea is searched as hex too, `privacy.contact_index` included), the log, every stand-in object and the envelopes, lower-cased, for the name, "zelda", the email, the street (also URL-encoded as `1%20canary%20way` and `1+canary+way`) and five phone spellings, each also as hex of both its original and its lower-case spelling, since hex digits do not fold with letter case (`5a656c6461` is "Zelda", `7a656c6461` is "zelda"); the log, the stub, `ops.audit_log`, `core.task` and the stream's audit and request objects must each hold something, so an empty scan cannot pass. Checked by mutation during the build: a sentinel logged at the error site and a table holding the name as bytes, in lower and in original case, each fail the test. The test crate gains `askhava-fixtures` (added to `[workspace.dependencies]` as a path dependency) and dev-dependencies `askhava-adapters`, `askhava-ops`, `base64`, `jiff`, `secrecy`, `sentry`, `serde_json`, `sha2`, `sqlx`, `tower-http`, `tracing` and `tracing-subscriber`, all already approved; no new library. The test file is about 290 lines against the prompt's 250-line budget, since `rustfmt` spreads the setup. Source: `docs/spec/privacy.md:20`; `docs/spec/privacy.md:23`; `docs/test-design.md:456`; D-109; D-647; D-736.
- **D-800** Question (T023, October 30, 2026): how does the scrubber read AI-002's "up to two words unless the first is on a common-words list in settings", and where does that list live while no owner-settings store exists? Choice: after a trigger phrase the first word is removed when it is letters only and not a common word; the second is removed too when it is letters only, not a common word, and the first did not end in punctuation ("This is Dave, call…" loses only "Dave"). Besides AI-002's phrases the scrubber also triggers on "i am", "my name's" and TD-AI-09's "mi nombre es", and on one or two words that end a message after a sign-off ("Thanks,", "Gracias,", "regards", a dash). `CommonWords` is passed in by the caller; `DEFAULT_COMMON_WORDS` (English and Spanish fillers and the -ing words that follow "I'm" or "it's") is the default until the owner setting exists, when the composition passes the setting's list instead. Over-removal of an uncommon word ("it's flooding" loses "flooding") is accepted: AI-020 measures recall on contact tokens, and a missed name is the costlier error. Street names are removed with their suffix (up to three words before "St", "Way" and the like, and the house number before them) or after "calle", "avenida" or "camino"; the number after "code", "gate", "pin", "código" or "clave" is removed. The committed corpus is 57 snippets in 4 frames (228 cases) in `app/privacy/src/tests/scrub.rs`; it scores 100% today and fails `Ci` below 99%. Source: `docs/spec/ai.md:6`, `docs/spec/ai.md:24`, D-146.
- **D-801** Question (T023, October 30, 2026): D-093 and PRIV-026 have the inbound reader store the raw text in `privacy.message_body` and the contact details a person states in the contact record, but no task in `kit/tasks.json` owns a migration creating `privacy.message_body`, and T023 owns no migration. Choice: T023 builds the reader as pure code: `read_inbound` and `read_inbound_email` return flags and `ScrubbedText` (and for email the SPF, DKIM and DMARC results, the standing and the sender's blind index) and never return the raw text or the sender's address; names a person states are kept in the caller's opaque `NameMemory` (Debug prints a count only) so later turns lose them (AI-020). The table, the raw-body write, the stated-detail write to `privacy.contact` and TD-PRIV-11's day-31 and "nowhere outside `privacy.message_body`" storage cases are a plan gap flagged for the runner: they need a task owning a `privacy` migration (T092's purge task is the natural owner, as it cuts the body at 30 days). Source: `docs/spec/privacy.md:30`, `docs/architecture.md` section 8 (the inbound flow), D-093.
- **D-802** Question (T023, October 30, 2026): what does the signed inbound email webhook carry, what does "a sender that fails them" mean, and how is the email blind index derived "per purpose" when `IndexPurpose` has one `Email` purpose and T023 does not own `models.rs`? Choice: the signature is Resend's Svix scheme as `stand_ins/resend.py` models it (`svix-id`, `svix-timestamp`, `svix-signature` with `v1,<base64 HMAC-SHA256>` over `<id>.<timestamp>.<body>`, key from `whsec_`), compared in constant time, refused more than 300 seconds from now. The body shape `{"type":"email.received","data":{"from","text","auth":{"spf","dkim","dmarc"}}}` is an assumption the stand-in does not yet serve; T133 (Resend test mode) checks it against the provider's inbound payload and adjusts the private parsing types only. A sender is authenticated only when SPF, DKIM and DMARC all pass; any other result (fail, none, softfail) is `Standing::OptOutOnly`, the stricter reading. The sender address (from `Name <a@b>` or `a@b`, lower-cased) is hashed under the `email` index key with a `business|` or `homeowner|` prefix, so the two match targets never share a digest; `email_index` gives the stored side the same derivation. A separate `IndexPurpose` per target can replace the prefix in a task that owns `models.rs`. Source: `docs/spec/privacy.md:30`, `stand_ins/resend.py:7`.
- **D-803** Question (T023 review, October 30, 2026): which phone spellings, house numbers and names did the first scrubber miss, and how far does it go to catch them? Choice: number words now include the teens and tens in English and Spanish ("eleven", "quince", "fifty", "veinti"); a tens word joined to a unit word spells two digits ("twenty-eight" is 28) and alone spells two ("twenty" is 20); "double", "doble" and "triple" repeat the next token's digits ("double five" is 55); inside a token holding a digit, or as a one-letter token, "o" reads as 0 and "l" as 1 ("555 O1l3"). A house number of 3 to 6 digits followed by one or two capitalised (not all-capitals), uncommon words is removed with them ("I'm at 2150 Mesquite"); all-capitals words are left so commands like "CLOSE 1042 YES" survive. Every word removed after a trigger phrase is remembered, not only the first ("my name is Rosa Tester" later removes "Tester" alone). Every vault-name word of 2 or more letters is removed even when it is on the common-words list ("Joy Early" removes "early"): AI-003 names the vault name without exception, and over-removal is the cheaper error (D-800). The corpus grows to 63 snippets (252 cases). Source: `docs/spec/ai.md:6`, `docs/spec/ai.md:7`, `docs/spec/ai.md:24`, D-800.
- **D-804** Question (T023 review, October 30, 2026): how does the inbound email reader treat a missing auth block, an opt-out word followed by a signature or quoted reply, a failed sender's HELP or START word, and a repeated delivery? Choice: a payload with no `auth` block, or with a result missing, reads as not passing, so `Standing::OptOutOnly` (the stricter reading of PRIV-026; refusing it would also drop the opt-out). An email opts out when its whole body or its first non-empty line is one opt-out word ("Cancel" above "Sent from my phone" and a quote); "cancel my visit" does not, and the opt-out flag never closes a job (CON-008). For an `OptOutOnly` sender the HELP and START flags are cleared, so by construction only the opt-out can act; the emergency flag stays, as it only triggers a safety notice and changes nothing. `read_inbound_email` does not deduplicate: the caller (the `messaging` webhook handler) drops a repeated `svix-id` before calling, as it does for every webhook (`messaging.webhook_event`). Source: `docs/spec/privacy.md:30`, D-802.
- **D-805** Question (T031, October 30, 2026): JOB-003 says every waiting status has a timeout, and `docs/architecture.md` section 6 times several of them from events the `jobs` crate cannot see yet (Payment pending from a decline, Connected from the later of the release and the visit date, the day-14 check-in), so what timer does `jobs` set? Choice: on every entry into a waiting status `jobs` queues one backstop timer counted from the entry (`rules::timeout`, values in `JobStatus::wait`): Intake 72 hours → Closed early; Open 6 p.m. Arizona time the next day → No quotes yet; No quotes yet 5 days → Closed; Quotes ready 3 days → Closed (restarted on every entry, JOB-025); Awaiting confirm 4 business hours → Quotes ready; Payment pending 1 business hour → Quotes ready; both 60 clock minutes on an emergency job (PICK-044); Connected 21 days (day 14 plus 7) → Closed. The Intake 24-hour reminder, the Connected call check and check-ins, and the D-140 early close are later tasks' timers, which move the job through `move_to` like any other move. Corrected after the fresh-eyes review: a backstop from entry is not always a safe outer bound, because the spec counts several of these waits from a later event or extends or pauses them (Intake's 72 hours from the last homeowner reply, INT-019; Payment pending's hour from the decline, JOB-014 and FEE-020, its 4 hours while Stripe is down, FEE-018, and its pause in safe mode, FEE-038; Awaiting confirm's HOLD and away time, PICK-043 and BIZ-034; Connected's day-14 check-in from the later of the release and the earliest visit, JOB-015), so the earlier wording "a later, finer timer only ever fires first" was wrong. The values stay as the defaults from entry, and the task that owns each of those events restarts the wait from it with `restart_timer` (D-807), which supersedes the timer from entry; until those tasks land, no such event can happen in the app. Reason: a timer from entry keeps JOB-003 true for every waiting status now, and one restart call per event is smaller and safer than guessing longer backstops.
- **D-806** Question (T031, October 30, 2026): how does a timer know the job moved on (JOB-006), including a job that left a status and came back to it (Quotes ready restarts its 3 days, JOB-025), and how is a refused move "logged as a bug" (JOB-002)? Choice: `jobs.job.version` rises by one on every move; a timer's `core.task` payload holds the job ID, status and version (IDs and code names only), its dedupe key is `jobs.timeout.<job>.<version>`, and `run_timer` does nothing unless the version still matches; its move is the same guarded update fenced on status and version and is stamped at the timer's due time, not the worker's clock, so a late worker still times the next status from the right instant. A refused move returns `JobsError::RefusedMove` before anything is read or written and is logged once with `tracing::error!` (which reaches Sentry), not as an `ops.alert` row, since the caller's transaction may roll back and take the row with it. The two times can differ: `jobs.job.status_at` and the `jobs.status_history` row carry the move's instant (the timer's due time for a timer move), while the `ops.audit_log` row's `at` is the database's `now()` at commit (`AuditEntry` takes no instant), so for a late worker the audit row is later than the history row; the history row is the lifecycle's time of record and the audit row records when the change was written. Reason: the version is the one fact that distinguishes a re-entered status from the original, and stamping at the due time keeps replays deterministic.
- **D-807** Question (T031 second pass, October 30, 2026, after the fresh-eyes review): how does a later task count a waiting status's timer from an event after the entry, or extend or pause it (INT-019, JOB-014, JOB-015, FEE-018, FEE-020, FEE-038, PICK-043, BIZ-034), when `core` offers no way to delete or move a queued `core.task`? Options weighed: (a) lengthen the backstops to cover every extension: no finite value covers an open-ended pause, and it would break JOB-003's intent; (b) drop the backstop for those statuses: breaks JOB-003 now; (c) a timer version on the job. Choice (c): `jobs.job` gains `timer_from` (the instant the current wait counts from; set to the move's instant on every move) and `timer_version` (bumped by every restart); `jobs::api::restart_timer(db, id, (status, from))` updates both only if the job is still in `status` and `from` is not before the current `timer_from` (a restart never shortens a wait), and queues the new timer in the same transaction with payload `{job, status, version, timer}` and dedupe key `jobs.timeout.<job>.<version>.<timer>`. `run_timer` computes the due time from `timer_from` and does nothing unless both the version and the timer version still match; its move is fenced on both. A pause is a restart at `timer_from` plus the paused time. A restart writes no audit row: the status does not change (JOB-005 covers status changes). Migration 0031 is not yet on `main`, so the columns join it rather than a new migration. Tested by `a_restarted_wait_supersedes_the_pending_timer`. Reason: the smallest change inside `jobs` that lets each later task re-time a pending wait without touching `core`.
- **D-808** Question (T031 second pass, October 30, 2026): the review asked for the audit-per-change property to run against the database, a `SET ROLE` proof that `jobs.status_history` is append-only, and a check that a refused move is logged. Choice: `prop_job_machine.rs::every_applied_move_writes_one_audit_row` draws 24 deterministic random event runs from proptest's `TestRunner` (no shrinking, since the case runs inside `#[sqlx::test]`) and drives each through `move_to` on the database, comparing the `status_changed` audit rows and the history rows with the oracle's changes; the in-memory machine stays for arrows and clock advances. `transitions.rs::the_app_role_cannot_rewrite_the_history` runs `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `TRUNCATE` on the history as `askhava_app` and expects each refused (postgres brain P5). The refused-move test counts error-level events through a `tracing-subscriber` layer set as the thread's default; `tracing-subscriber` becomes a dev-dependency of `askhava-jobs` (already approved and in the workspace, no new library). Reason: each property is now proved where it can fail.
- **D-809** Question (T031, October 30, 2026): the task prompt's size budget is 10 files and 400 changed lines; the change is about 25 files and about 1,500 lines. Why? Choice: accept the overrun and record it. A new crate needs its `Cargo.toml`, `CLAUDE.md`, `sqlx.toml`, `lib.rs`, test module file and `.sqlx/` query files besides the ten owned files, and the second pass added the restart path (D-807) and three tests (D-808); rustfmt spreads the async database tests. Nothing was split out because the statuses, moves, history and timers only work together. Reason: the budget is a guide for small pull requests (`BUILD_BRIEF.md:485`); splitting the state machine would leave a half-working module on `main`.
- **D-815** Question (T014, October 30, 2026): how are card, quote, pick and link IDs derived, and what does the shared webhook dedupe helper look like when `core` cannot write another module's table (CARD-017, PICK-028, SEC-017, SEC-037, SEC-039, D-491)? Choice: `core::ids` keys HMAC-SHA-256 with an `IdSecret` (the `ID_SECRET` value and its version, refused under 32 bytes or at version 0) over the version, a kind label (`id.card`, `id.quote`, `id.pick`, `link.quote_page`, `link.action`, `link.photo`) and the record IDs, every field length-prefixed; a record ID is the first 128 bits as a UUID (card and quote from job and business, pick from job and quote); a link token is all 256 bits over the record ID and a 16-byte salt from the OS source, as 64 hex digits, stored only as its SHA-256. `core::webhooks` gives `Dedupe::from_returning` (the `Guarded` pattern of D-491) and `EventKey` (1 to 128 of `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]` per part, pairs joined by `:`), and documents the table shape `(source, event_key, received_at)` with the `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING` insert each module writes. The quote-page token lives in `jobs.quote_token` (migration 0032) with `jobs::api::quote_token::{issue, revoke, resolve}`: one live row per job, issue revokes the old row in the same transaction, both audited. Reason: SEC-037's own wording (`docs/spec/security.md:41`) and the kernel design of `docs/architecture.md` section 5; the version in the HMAC input keeps a rotated secret from colliding with the old one.
- **D-816** Question (T014, October 30, 2026): `core` now names `hmac`, `sha2` and `rand`; are they new libraries? Choice: no new crate: all three are already pinned in `[workspace.dependencies]` and listed in `kit/allowed_crates.txt` (`docs/architecture.md` section 11), and `rand 0.10.3` was already in `Cargo.lock`; `core` uses only `rand::rngs::SysRng` (the operating system's source) through `TryRng::try_fill_bytes`, so a failing source is an error, never a weak salt. Reason: `BUILD_BRIEF.md:122` asks for an entry only for a new library; this records the use.
- **D-817** Question (T014, October 30, 2026): SEC-037 says the per-record salt is written to the off-database stream, but `ops::api::StreamEvent` has only `Audit`, `Request` and `AiReading`, and an audit row may hold only code names and record IDs (PRIV-028), so `jobs` has no way to put a salt on the stream; `ops` and `server`'s stream writer are not this task's files. Choice: issue and revoke each write an audit row (`quote_token_issued`, `quote_token_revoked` on the `jobs.job`) that reaches the stream, and the salt stays in `jobs.quote_token`, from which `link_token` reproduces the token (tested); the copy of the salt itself is left for a follow-up that adds a salt-carrying stream event to `ops` and its writer in `server` (for example `StreamEvent::LinkSalt { record, salt }`), before the replay task (T110) relies on it. Reason: changing `ops` and `server` is outside the owned files (`BUILD_BRIEF.md:485`); the gap is recorded rather than worked around with a misuse of the audit columns.
- **D-818** Question (T014, October 30, 2026): the task prompt's size budget is 7 files and 350 changed lines; the change is 23 files and about 950 lines. Why? Choice: accept the overrun and record it. The seven owned files hold about 750 lines, a third of them tests that rustfmt spreads out, plus the `//!` and `///` comments `docs/code-docs.md` requires; the rest are the shared wiring (`lib.rs`, `api.rs`, `tests/mod.rs`, two `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, three `.sqlx/` query files) and the crate guides and decision log. Nothing was split out because the ID derivation, the token store and the dedupe helper are each tested end to end here. Reason: the budget is a guide for small pull requests (`BUILD_BRIEF.md:485`), as in D-809.
- **D-819** Question (T014 second pass, October 30, 2026, after the review): a card, quote or pick ID is HMAC over the `ID_SECRET` version as well as the record IDs (D-815), so rotating the secret to a new version would give the same job and business a different ID; which one is right, and what must replay do? Choice: a derived ID is pinned to the secret version in force when the record was made. Nothing re-derives a stored ID after a rotation: the stored ID is the record's identity from then on, and a rotation only changes the IDs of records made after it. Replay (T110) must derive each record's ID with the version in force at that record's original time, so it keeps every old version's key until no record made under it can be replayed, and keeps the rotation instant (or the version on each event) on the off-database stream; link tokens already store their `key_version` per row.
